brief: September US nonfarm payrolls rose 29k, below the 80k forecast and far under August's slightly-revised 133k, which the note frames as mean reversion after an erratically strong prior print exciting hawks, so a weak one should excite doves. Unemployment rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, driven by stronger labor-force participation, which the note calls generally a good thing. Wage growth was subdued at 0.1% MoM. Sector detail showed mild positive job growth almost everywhere; only tech, finance, business services and government posted negligible declines, which the note reads as noise rather than a genuine downturn. Conclusion: the US labor market has turned the corner in 2026, but the reacceleration is not fast enough to push the Fed toward aggressive hiking. After September's hike, an October move was already unlikely, now confirmed by various Fed officials this week; the bond market agrees, and pressure on forward rates has eased. Looking to 2027, the note expects further labor-market improvement to keep the Fed on a quarterly hiking path, but says terminal rate pricing now looks about right.
